lessons.title: Why food spoils – microbes
lessons.hook: Disha opened a lunch box forgotten since Friday. **A bad smell and coloured patches on her uttapam!** What happened? Mystery #1 begins.

core.def: Tiny living things seen only with a microscope. Found in soil, water, air, plants, animals and inside us.
Coloured patches on food – a colony of thousands of microbes.
Moisture, air and the right temperature. Remove any one and they stop growing.
Can give an upset stomach.

explain: Bread left out for two days got mould, but pickles covered with oil stayed good for two months.
Some microbes are helpful – they make curd and help digestion.

example.q: Why do some foods spoil faster than others? (2 marks)
steps: Microbes grow on food when they get moisture, air and the right temperature.
Foods kept dry, covered with oil or kept cold spoil slowly, like Paati’s pickle.
example.answer: Moisture, air and warmth help microbes; removing them slows spoiling.

mistakes: Forgetting one of the three needs (moisture, air, temperature).
lessons.tip: Learn the three needs as M-A-T: Moisture, Air, Temperature.
lessons.memory: Microbes need a MAT to grow!

lessons.title: Saving food – preservation
lessons.hook: Chillies drying on the balcony, oil poured over pickles, milk in the fridge. **Every family is fighting microbes!** Preservation keeps food safe for longer.

core.def: Removes moisture – chillies, papad, aam papad, khakhra, dried fish.
Oil keeps out air – lemon and mango pickles.
Cold slows microbes – milk, vegetables, butter.
Old methods still used today – pepper was so popular that Vasco da Gama came to India for it.
Air-tight cans in factories keep microbes out.
Butter is heated; water separates and evaporates – ghee needs no fridge.

explain: Matkas (clay pots) keep water cool without electricity.
Even insects preserve food – hunting wasps store food for their larvae.

example.q: Name three ways of preserving food with one example each. (3 marks)
steps: Drying in the Sun – chilli powder.
Keeping in a fridge – milk and vegetables.

mistakes: Mixing up why each method works (drying = no moisture, oil = no air, cold = slow microbes).
lessons.tip: For every method, say WHAT it removes.
lessons.memory: Dry it, oil it, chill it, can it!

lessons.title: Good microbes, seasonal food
lessons.hook: Not all microbes are villains! **Some of them make our idlis fluffy and our curd tasty.**

core.def: Microbes in the air make the batter rise and become fluffy.
A spoonful of old curd in warm milk – microbes do the rest.
Microbes in curd and buttermilk help the good microbes in our stomach. See a doctor if it is severe.
Taste best in their season, e.g. amla in winter, jamun in summer; local fruits are fresher.

explain: Fermented rice (pakhala, kanji) cools the body and has good bacteria.
Bad eating habits can also cause indigestion (Finding #8).

example.q: Give two ways in which microbes are useful to us. (2 marks)
steps: They make idli batter rise and turn milk into curd.

mistakes: Forgetting that some microbes are helpful.
lessons.tip: When asked ‘useful microbes’, write food + digestion.
lessons.memory: Good microbes: curd, idli, happy tummy!

lessons.title: Chew right – teeth and hygiene
lessons.hook: Disha looked in the mirror and said **“Aaaaah!”** Different teeth, different jobs – and saliva joins in too.

core.def: Cut food.
Tear food.
Crush food.
Grind food.
Chewing well releases saliva, which helps digest food.
Rinse after eating, brush regularly, eat fewer sweets; see a dentist for a cavity or toothache.
Eat slowly, take small mouthfuls, do not talk or laugh with food in your mouth.

explain: Eating with hands helps you feel the texture of food and prepares your stomach for digestion.

lessons.tip: Point to your own teeth from front to back while saying cut–tear–crush–grind.

revision: **Microbes** are tiny living things everywhere; **mould** is a colony of them.
Microbes need **moisture, air and the right temperature**.
Preserve food by **drying, oiling, cooling, salt/sugar, canning**.
**Ghee** keeps without a fridge because its water is removed.
**Good microbes** make curd and idli and help digestion.
Teeth: **incisors cut, canines tear, premolars crush, molars grind**; chew well to avoid choking.

sections.title: Match-the-following tips
items: First match the ones you are sure of.
For preservation, ask: does it remove moisture, air or warmth?
Check every item is used once.

sections.title: Writing answers that score
items: Read the question twice and underline the key word (why, how, name, list).
Answer in full sentences using words from the book – e.g. ‘Microbes need moisture, air and the right temperature to grow.’
For ‘why’ questions, give the reason with ‘because’.
For 2–3 mark answers, write 2–3 separate points.
Add one example from the chapter (Godavari, Disha’s pickle, the green school) to show you understand.
Draw and label a simple diagram when it helps – the water cycle, types of teeth, the river’s journey.

sections.title: The day before the test
items: Read the key facts sheet aloud once.
Do the Play & learn activities again – if you get every card right first time, you are ready.
Take one Check knowledge quiz at Hard level.

checklist: I can explain why food spoils.
I can name what microbes need to grow.
I can match foods with their preservation method.
I can give two uses of good microbes.
I can name the four types of teeth and their jobs.
exam.paperTitle: How this chapter is usually tested
exam.paperNote: Typical Class V school test pattern (1-mark MCQ, fill in the blanks, true/false and matching; 2–3 mark short answers; activity-based questions). Your school’s paper may differ slightly.

method: Built on how children learn best: start with a story or activity, sort and match ideas with your hands, say answers aloud before checking (active recall), and come back after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
